## Overview

This Adyen guide documents a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) route for a custom Web card integration in which the merchant implements its own UI. It uses a third-party JWT library and an Adyen-provided, merchant-account-specific X.509 certificate-derived public key to encrypt card details on the shopper device before the encrypted payload is sent through the merchant server in a `/payments` request.

## Key takeaways

- The route is for a Web API-only integration whose frontend has access to unencrypted card details, including the page's examples of a multiple-payment-service-provider setup or a merchant risk engine.
- The stated prerequisites include the Checkout webservice API-credential role, the Customer Area **Manage API credentials** role, a backend able to make a payment, and the downloaded client-side-encryption public key as an X.509 certificate.
- The merchant derives a JSON Web Key (JWK) from the merchant-account-specific certificate, encrypts the card details on the client, sends the compact JWE to its server, and submits it as `paymentMethod.encryptedCard` in `/payments`.
- Adyen says it does not share decryption keys, so only Adyen can decrypt the encrypted card details for payment processing. The guide advises using algorithms that meet Adyen's security standards; its JOSE example sets `alg` to `RSA-OAEP-256` and `enc` to `A256GCM`.

> [!warning] PCI and evidence boundary
> The page directs implementers to check their PCI DSS requirements and explicitly describes a frontend that can access unencrypted card details. JWE encryption is therefore not evidence that an integration is PCI-compliant or outside PCI scope. This unversioned documentation snapshot also does not prove current account or role eligibility, certificate validity, library security, successful decryption, payment authorization, capture, settlement, or fulfillment safety.

quotes.text: | **Limitations**                                                           | Make sure to check your PCI DSS requirements in the [PCI DSS compliance guide](/development-resources/pci-dss-compliance-guide).                                                                                            |

We offer multiple ways for you to accept [card payments](/payment-methods/cards) for different use cases and different PCI compliance levels. Card detail encryption with JWE is for when you want to have access to the unencrypted card details from your frontend, for example when:

In a JWE setup, you use a [third-party JWT library](https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript) to encrypt card details as a JSON Web Token. The encrypted details can be safely passed to your server, where you can use them for a [/payments](https://docs.adyen.com/api-explorer/Checkout/latest/post/payments) request. We never share decryption keys, so once you encrypt card details only Adyen can decrypt them to process your payment.

1. You download your merchant account-specific X.509 certificate from the [Customer Area](https://ca-test.adyen.com/).
2. You compute your JSON Web Key (JWK) from your X.509 certificate.
3. Your shopper enters their card details in your checkout.
4. You encrypt the card details on the client side using your JWK key.
5. You pass the encrypted card details to your server.
6. You make a [/payments](https://docs.adyen.com/api-explorer/Checkout/latest/post/payments) request using the encrypted card details.

## Definition

Adyen's JWE card-encryption route supports a custom Web API-only integration in which the merchant's own frontend can access unencrypted card details. The frontend uses a third-party JWT library and a public key derived from a merchant-account-specific X.509 certificate to encrypt the card details on the shopper device. The merchant passes the compact JWE to its server, which supplies it as `paymentMethod.encryptedCard` in a `/payments` request; Adyen says it does not share the decryption keys, so only Adyen can decrypt the payload for payment processing. [[source-adyen-docs-online-payments-card-encryption-with-jwe]]

## Access and compliance boundaries

The retained guide requires a Web API-only integration, the Checkout webservice API-credential role, the Customer Area **Manage API credentials** role, a backend able to make a payment, and the downloaded client-side-encryption certificate. These access prerequisites connect to [[adyen-api-access]], but the encryption lifecycle is a separate concept. Because the custom frontend can access unencrypted card details and the guide tells implementers to check PCI DSS requirements, encryption does not by itself establish PCI compliance or reduced scope. The snapshot also does not prove current eligibility, certificate validity, successful decryption, payment authorization, capture, settlement, or fulfillment safety.
